newsitem.title: USA: Some funds take lazy way to profits.
newsitem.headline: Some funds take lazy way to profits.

text.p: Why do so many investors spend so much time trying to pick the right mutual funds? They want to outperform the financial markets, and they figure the right fund will help them reach that target.
That may be true. But it's hard to find the right fund.
In fact, only about three in 10 stock funds have kept pace with market benchmarks such as the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks over the past decade. The rest have trailed the market.

Some funds lag the market's performance because of the expenses they charge shareholders, which come out of investment returns. The fund sponsors often justify those costs by saying they will use the money to hire researchers and stock pickers who can generate strong performance.
So where's the performance? True, there are some long-term winners among the funds available to investors. Names such as Brandywine and Mutual Shares come to mind.
But even long-term winners sometimes stumble. Often, their success attracts so much money that even the best managers cannot find enough good stocks to buy.

Consider the recent record of the Magellan Fund, with assets of about $55 billion the nation's largest mutual fund. The fund has gained just 11.5 percent since 1993, vs. a 20.9 percent return for the S&P 500.
Other long-term winners stumble when their managers make big bets that turn out badly.

For example, Crabbe Huson Special was the top-ranked aggressive growth fund at the beginning of 1995. But manager Jim Crabbe began betting technology stocks would fall. When they rallied instead, the fund's returns suffered and it has suffered a 1.9 percent loss so far this year.
Other funds lose managers and replace them with less seasoned stock pickers. Still others lag when their investment style goes out of fashion.
So, finding funds that can consistently beat the market -- or even keep pace with it -- is a tall order. That's why many investors choose index funds.
Index funds aim to match the market's performance, no more and no less. They do so by investing in a portfolio of stocks or other issues that reflect the make-up of an index such as the S&P 500.
Thus, there's no call for brilliant stock picks. The manager simply assures that the fund's portfolio remains similar to that of the appropriate index.
Index fund shareholders don't have to worry that their funds will make big bets on the wrong market sectors.

Better yet, shareholders get to keep more of their index funds' returns, because the funds are usually cheap to run. Expenses average about 0.5 percent of assets, compared to 1.5 percent or so for the typical actively managed stock fund.
Over the past three years, index funds that seek to match the S&P 500 have gained 20.1 percent, compared to 16.8 percent for the typical equity fund and 20.9 percent for the index itself.

How to choose an index fund? Start by picking your index. The S&P 500 represents the performance of large U.S. companies. It has inspired the most index funds, and one of them can form a solid core for your stock portfolio.

Beyond that, you might choose a fund that mirrors a small company stock index such as the Russell 2000. A diversified portfolio should also include overseas stocks, represented by international indexes such as the Morgan Stanley EAFE Index.
Bond investors can find funds that track the Lehman Brothers Aggregate Bond Index, the Salomon Brothers World Government Bond Index or other bond market gauges.

Another concern is cost. The Vanguard Group (800-662-7447) offers some of the lowest-cost index funds, which could boost your return each year. Even modest annual differences of half a point or so can mean big savings over time.

For example, you might start with the Seven Seas S&P 500 index (0.19 percent expenses; $1,000 minimum investment; 800-647-7327), and add diversification via the Schwab Small Cap Index (0.68 percent; $1,000 minimum; 800-266-5623), which tracks an index of small company shares.

For international stocks, investors can choose the new Vanguard Total International Portfolio (roughly 0.38 percent expenses; $3,000 minimum). Unlike other international index funds, this one holds a mix of stocks from established and emerging stock markets; thus, it offers better diversification and more growth potential, along with an extra dollop of risk.

Finally, bond investors can choose from several Vanguard entries, including Vanguard Total Bond Market (0.20 percent; $3,000 minimum), which tracks The Lehman Brothers Aggregate Bond Index, or Vanguard Bond Index Short Term (0.20 percent; $3,000 minimum), which mirrors the performance of government and corporate bonds with maturities of one to five years as measured by the Lehman Brothers Mutual Fund Short-Term Bond Index.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
